addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- qemu-runner: Use this agent when you need to run a RISC-V ELF binary through Andes QEMU and get its output. Always use this agent instead of running QEMU directly, as it handles the semihosting fd 9 output capture quirk in Claude Code's sandbox.

Examples:

- assistant: *builds a test binary*
  assistant: "Let me use the qemu-runner agent to execute the binary and check the output"

- user: "Run this ELF at VLEN=512"
  assistant: "I'll use the qemu-runner agent to run it" (Tools: Bash, Read) (Tools: Bash)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- iree-optimizer: Agentic per-dispatch tile-size tuner for IREE CPU codegen on RISC-V. Keeps IREE's chosen pipeline (CPUDoubleTilingExpert / CPUConvTileAndDecomposeExpert / CPUBufferOpsTileAndVectorize) and only overrides the root linalg op's lowering_config<tile_sizes = [...]>. Each round reads the best-so-far RISC-V assembly (LMUL, VLmax, register spills) to ground the next tile-size proposal; pre-compile divisibility gate ensures tiles divide their parent extents (no tail loop); a post-compile check of the IR after iree-codegen-generic-vectorization confirms no tail/masked main path. Compiles via iree_tuner.py, benchmarks on FPGA, iterates. Use whenever the user mentions tuning IREE dispatch tile sizes, agentic tile search, or wants to replace GA-based tile-size search with LLM-driven search. 1228	gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1234' my.elf
1229	```
1230	Default port: 1234. Override with `--gdb-port PORT`.
1231	
1232	**cycle model** -- resets and **halts** the hart (like QEMU's `-S`), opens vsim's
1233	JTAG bitbang port in the background, waits for it to come up, then execs `$ICEMAN`
1234	-- your JTAG debug server -- in the foreground:
1235	```sh
1236	export ICEMAN=/path/to/jtag-debug-server      # see note
1237	./andes-sim run --model cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium my.elf
1238	# then point GDB at the server's gdb port (OpenOCD's default is 1111):
1239	gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1111' my.elf
1240	```
1241	`--gdb-port PORT` sets vsim's JTAG bitbang port (default `9104`); GDB itself
1242	connects to the **server's own** gdb port, not this one. The hart starts halted,
1243	so the debugger attaches to a stopped core -- set breakpoints, then `continue`.
1244	
1245	`$ICEMAN` is whichever JTAG debug server you point it at; it must speak the
1246	OpenOCD `remote_bitbang` protocol to vsim's port. A current **OpenOCD (0.12+)**
1247	works -- a one-line `$ICEMAN` wrapper can just `exec openocd -f <cfg>`, where
1248	`<cfg>` selects `adapter driver remote_bitbang` at `remote_bitbang port 9104`,
1249	a generic `riscv` target, and a `gdb_port`. A full worked example is in
1250	`docs/andes_sim_demo.ipynb` ("7. Debug with GDB"). **Note:** Andes ICEman's
1251	*own* bundled OpenOCD 0.10 has a `remote_bitbang` bug that crashes against vsim's
1252	DTM, so point `$ICEMAN` at a modern OpenOCD rather than the bundled one.
1253	
1254	`--gdb` is not supported with `--model hybrid` (the handoff pipeline cannot pause for interactive debugging).

gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1234' my.elf
```
Default port: 1234. Override with `--gdb-port PORT`.

**cycle model** -- resets and **halts** the hart (like QEMU's `-S`), opens vsim's
JTAG bitbang port in the background, waits for it to come up, then execs `$ICEMAN`
-- your JTAG debug server -- in the foreground:
```sh
export ICEMAN=/path/to/jtag-debug-server      # see note
./andes-sim run --model cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium my.elf
# then point GDB at the server's gdb port (OpenOCD's default is 1111):
gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1111' my.elf
```
`--gdb-port PORT` sets vsim's JTAG bitbang port (default `9104`); GDB itself
connects to the **server's own** gdb port, not this one. The hart starts halted,
so the debugger attaches to a stopped core -- set breakpoints, then `continue`.

`$ICEMAN` is whichever JTAG debug server you point it at; it must speak the
OpenOCD `remote_bitbang` protocol to vsim's port. A current **OpenOCD (0.12+)**
works -- a one-line `$ICEMAN` wrapper can just `exec openocd -f <cfg>`, where
`<cfg>` selects `adapter driver remote_bitbang` at `remote_bitbang port 9104`,
a generic `riscv` target, and a `gdb_port`. A full worked example is in
`docs/andes_sim_demo.ipynb` ("7. Debug with GDB"). **Note:** Andes ICEman's
*own* bundled OpenOCD 0.10 has a `remote_bitbang` bug that crashes against vsim's
DTM, so point `$ICEMAN` at a modern OpenOCD rather than the bundled one.

`--gdb` is not supported with `--model hybrid` (the handoff pipeline cannot pause for interactive debugging).

**Root cause: the bundled OpenOCD 0.10 inside Andes ICEman has a `remote_bitbang` driver bug. This is already a known, documented issue in this repo** (`docs/USER_GUIDE.md:1250-1252`):

Your crash signature matches exactly:
- Banner says `0.11.0+dev` but the failing assertion path is `openocd-0.10.0/src/jtag/drivers/remote_bitbang.c:207` — that 0.10 source is the buggy bundled driver.
- `remote_bitbang_read_sample: Assertion !remote_bitbang_recv_buf_empty()` fires because that driver mishandles its receive buffer when reading a TDO sample from vsim's virtual DMI/DTM. `IOT instruction (core dumped)` = the SIGABRT from the failed `assert`.

It is not your `virtual_dmi.cfg` and not a missing server — it's the debug client.

```sh

./andes-sim run --model cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium my.elf
gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1111' my.elf   # OpenOCD's gdb port
```

Worked example: `docs/andes_sim_demo.ipynb` section "7. Debug with GDB".

aiTitle: Fix ICEman remote bitbang assertion failure

content.text:
Confirmed the root cause. `driver/cmd_run.cpp:207`:

```cpp
return exec_passthrough({iceman, "-Z", "v5"});
```

The framework **always** execs `$ICEMAN -Z v5`. `-Z v5` is an Andes-ICEman-only flag (select the V5 RISC-V arch). Your `$ICEMAN` now resolves to a modern OpenOCD 0.12 build, which has no `-Z` option, so it aborts with `invalid option -- 'Z'`.

Note the framework passes **only** `-Z v5` — no `-f <cfg>`, no port. So even if `-Z` were accepted, a bare `openocd` still wouldn't know to use `remote_bitbang` on 9104. That gap is intentional: per `docs/USER_GUIDE.md:1247`, `$ICEMAN` is meant to be a **wrapper that does `exec openocd -f <cfg>` and drops the framework's args** (it does not forward `"$@"`). You pointed `$ICEMAN` straight at the openocd binary (or a wrapper that forwards args), so `-Z v5` leaked through.

## Fix: make `$ICEMAN` a wrapper that ignores `-Z v5`

The repo already ships the config (`verilator/tools/openocd-rbb.cfg`, remote_bitbang @ 9104):

input.command: grep -n "exec_passthrough" driver/*.hpp driver/*.cpp 2>/dev/null | head; echo "---cfg has gdb_port?---"; grep -n "gdb_port\|remote_bitbang port\|3333\|1111" verilator/tools/openocd-rbb.cfg

content.text:
`exec_passthrough` just `execvp`s the argv as given — `argv = {iceman, "-Z", "v5"}`. So the wrapper must supply `-f <cfg>` itself and ignore the trailing `-Z v5`.

```sh
cat > ~/iceman-wrap.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# andes-sim execs us as "$ICEMAN -Z v5"; modern OpenOCD has no -Z.
# Drop the framework args and run OpenOCD with the remote_bitbang cfg.
exec openocd -f /home/nick/work/andes-sim/verilator/tools/openocd-rbb.cfg
EOF
chmod +x ~/iceman-wrap.sh
export ICEMAN=~/iceman-wrap.sh

./andes-sim run --model cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf
# then, in another shell:
gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :3333' hello.elf
```

GDB port note: `openocd-rbb.cfg` sets no `gdb_port`, so OpenOCD listens on its **default 3333** (the guide's "1111" is wrong / from a different cfg). Add `gdb_port 1111` to the cfg if you want that number.

---

1. **This is a real design wart in the framework**, not just your setup. `cmd_run.cpp:207` hardcodes the Andes-only `-Z v5` onto whatever `$ICEMAN` points at, while the docs tell you to use modern OpenOCD — which can't parse `-Z`. The only thing that bridges them is "your wrapper must silently eat the args." A cleaner fix would be to not inject `-Z v5` (or make the ICEman args configurable / env-driven).
